message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"f093852c1e0d5217f496896297f97030cb91d63e336acdbd86cf6de86b163bb3","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-or-class-c:lineage:54","source_registry_sha256":"ce8335c1d96ff7ed209bf236ba9a56fe92dfebd915bc0e2fa7fb830ee03f0f09","units":[{"unit_id":"sec09-u01","module_id":"sec09-m01","objective_ids":["sec09-u01"],"title":{"text":"Defensive driving and collisions","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Safe driving rests on awareness, and a defensive driver always knows the surroundings and possible escape routes.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Belt and child seat rules are exact, and the three collision escapes are what you use when a crash is close.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-F07","sec09-F11"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A car behind you is about to strike you, and the road ahead of you is open.","fact_ids":["sec09-F14"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Speeding up can be the best escape when a vehicle is about to strike you from behind and the road ahead is open enough to get clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F14","sec09-R20"]},"result":{"text":"You speed up into the open road ahead to get clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F14"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking stopping is always the only way to avoid a collision.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11"]},"correction":{"text":"The manual lists three ways to avoid a collision or soften it: stopping quickly, turning quickly and speeding up.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stop, turn or speed up.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A seven-year-old who is four feet tall rides with you. What must the child sit in?","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"answer":{"text":"An approved child safety seat.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"A child rides in an approved child safety seat until reaching eight years of age or four feet nine inches, and the adult belt must fit correctly.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Driving defensively","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stay aware at all times.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Know your escape routes.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Safe, responsible driving rests on staying aware of everything around you at all times and watching for situations that could turn dangerous. Defensive driving means adjusting for vehicle trouble, the road surface, bad weather, heavy traffic, poor lighting, and your own physical, mental and emotional state. A defensive driver keeps track of the surroundings and of possible escape routes at all times. This lesson builds on that idea, covering your view, safety belts, child safety seats, how to tell others what you plan to do, and the three ways to avoid a collision.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Safety belts","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every driver and passenger.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-F06"]},{"text":"All available seating positions.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-F06"]},{"text":"No slack, strap on the shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Oregon requires safety belts for every driver and every passenger in all available seating positions. That means every seat in the vehicle that has a belt, front or back. How you wear the belt matters too. Wear it with no slack in the lap part or the shoulder part. And never put the shoulder strap under your arm or behind your back. A belt that is loose, or a shoulder strap moved out of place, is not worn the way the manual requires. So buckle every person in every available seat, snug the belt, and keep the shoulder strap across the shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Child safety seats","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Child seat until eight years or four feet nine.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Adult belt must fit correctly.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Infants rear-facing until two.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Children have their own rules. A child must ride in an approved child safety seat until reaching eight years of age or a height of at least four feet nine inches, and the adult lap and shoulder belt must fit the child correctly. Infants have an extra rule: they must ride facing the rear until they are two years old. So there are two separate numbers to keep straight. Two years old is the rear-facing rule for infants. Eight years of age or four feet nine inches is the child safety seat rule, together with a correct fit for the adult belt.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Telling others your plans","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Collisions follow surprises.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},{"text":"Signal, brake lights, headlights.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},{"text":"Horn and hazard lights when needed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Collisions often happen because one driver fails to see another vehicle, or a driver does something others do not expect. So you make your plans known. You tell other drivers what you plan to do by signaling before changing direction or lanes, by showing your brake lights, by using your headlights, by using the horn as a reasonable warning, and by using hazard lights when needed. Each of these is a way to tell other drivers what you plan to do, and the manual names failing to see another vehicle and doing something unexpected as common causes of collisions.","fact_ids":["sec09-F09","sec09-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Three ways out","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop quickly.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"]},{"text":"Turn quickly.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"]},{"text":"Speed up.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"When a collision is close, the manual gives three ways to avoid it or soften its impact: stopping quickly, turning quickly and speeding up. Stopping quickly works when you have enough distance to stop, and your owner's manual explains how to use your vehicle's brakes properly. Most vehicles can turn away faster than they can stop, so if you cannot stop in time, steer away from the collision toward an escape route you spotted by scanning. And speeding up can be the best escape when a vehicle is about to strike you from behind or from the side and the road ahead is open enough to get clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Turning versus speeding up","fact_ids":["sec09-R20","sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Turning is usually quickest.","fact_ids":["sec09-R20","sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F12"]},{"text":"Speed up for threats from behind or beside.","fact_ids":["sec09-R20","sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap: picking the wrong escape for the threat. Turning away is usually the quickest escape because most vehicles turn faster than they stop. Speeding up is the choice when the threat comes from the side or from behind and the road ahead is open enough to get clear. Stopping quickly needs enough distance to stop. So match the escape to the situation. If a crash is ahead and you cannot stop in time, steer away toward your escape route. If a vehicle is about to strike you from behind or from the side, speeding up into open road may be the way out.","fact_ids":["sec09-R20","sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check on child seats","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Seven years old, four feet tall.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},{"text":"Which restraint?","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a seven-year-old who is four feet tall is riding in your car. What must the child sit in? The answer is an approved child safety seat. A child must ride in an approved child safety seat until reaching eight years of age or a height of at least four feet nine inches, and the adult lap and shoulder belt must fit the child correctly. This child has reached neither eight years nor four feet nine inches, so the child safety seat is still required. And for an infant, remember the separate rule of facing the rear until two years old.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Defensive habits together","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Clear view on every side.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"Belts, child seats, signals.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"Stop, turn or speed up.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"To pull this lesson together: stay aware of everything around you and keep track of possible escape routes. You must be able to see to the front, sides and rear, so never load or equip the vehicle in a way that blocks your view, and remember that window stickers or objects can cut into it. Buckle every driver and passenger with no slack, keep children in an approved child safety seat until eight years of age or four feet nine inches with a correct belt fit, and keep infants rear-facing until two. Signal your plans, and when a crash is close, stop, turn or speed up.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec09-u02","module_id":"sec09-m02","objective_ids":["sec09-u02"],"title":{"text":"Off the road and on alert","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Leaving the road by accident is survivable if you avoid the wrong reaction of panic and hard braking.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F17"]},{"text":"A drifting oncoming vehicle and a frightened animal call for different responses.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F22","sec09-R21"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"An oncoming car drifts across the center line into your lane on a two-lane road.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18"]},"reasoning":{"text":"You move as far right as you can, slow down and warn the driver with your horn or lights, and you never swerve into the opposing lane.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]},"result":{"text":"You steer toward the shoulder rather than the other lane, since the shoulder or ditch is usually safer than a head-on crash.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking the safest escape from a drifting car is to swerve into its empty lane.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19"]},"correction":{"text":"Never swerve into the opposing lane, since the drifting driver may jerk back into it; the shoulder or ditch is usually safer than a head-on crash.","fact_ids":["sec09-F19"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Right, slow, warn; never left.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Your right wheels drop off the pavement. What two things should you not do first?","fact_ids":["sec09-F15"]},"answer":{"text":"Do not panic and do not brake hard.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15"]},"rationale":{"text":"If your wheels leave the road, you avoid panic and hard braking and slow down until you can return safely.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F17"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"When things go wrong","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F18","sec09-F22"]},"lines":[{"text":"Wheels off the road.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F18","sec09-F22"]},{"text":"Drifting cars and animals.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F18","sec09-F22"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about three situations that call for a calm, specific response. The first is when your wheels leave the road. The second is when an oncoming vehicle drifts into your lane. The third is meeting animals, including a horseback rider or someone leading an animal. In each case the manual gives you a clear set of steps, and in each case the wrong instinct, such as braking hard, swerving into the other lane or honking, makes things worse. We will take the three situations in turn and then compare the two that most often get mixed up.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F18","sec09-F22"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Getting back on the road","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"No panic, no hard braking.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},{"text":"Firm grip, go straight.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},{"text":"Steer back gently.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"If your wheels leave the road, do not panic or brake hard. Slow down until you can return to the road safely. While you slow, hold the steering wheel firmly and keep the vehicle going straight. Then steer back onto the road with only as much front wheel turn as needed, because a sharp turn can carry you across the road into oncoming traffic. So the order is: stay calm, ease off and slow down, hold the wheel firmly and steer straight, and when it is safe, use a gentle turn to bring the vehicle back onto the road surface.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"A drifting oncoming vehicle","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Move far right and slow down.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]},{"text":"Warn with horn or lights.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]},{"text":"Shoulder beats a head-on crash.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"If an oncoming vehicle drifts into your lane, move as far right as you can, slow down, and warn the driver with your horn or lights. Never swerve into the opposing lane to dodge a drifting vehicle, since its driver may jerk back into that lane. If you have to leave your lane, heading for the shoulder or ditch is usually safer than a head-on crash. So your escape is always to the right side, away from the other vehicle's lane, while you slow down and use your horn or lights to get the other driver's attention. Right, slow and warn is the full response.","fact_ids":["sec09-F18","sec09-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Animals on the road","fact_ids":["sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Watch for animal crossing signs.","fact_ids":["sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"Stop for a raised hand.","fact_ids":["sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"No loud noises.","fact_ids":["sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Watch for animal crossing signs and be ready to brake or slow down when passing an animal. If you hit and injure a domestic animal, stop, make a reasonable effort to check its injuries, and report it right away to the owner, or to local law enforcement if the owner cannot be found. Stop for a horseback rider or someone leading an animal who raises a hand, or when the animal is clearly frightened, unless stopping would cause a collision; a raised hand signals a frightened animal. And do not honk or make other loud, sudden noises near a horse or other animal on the road.","fact_ids":["sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Car versus horse","fact_ids":["sec09-R21","sec09-F18","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Drifting car: move right and warn.","fact_ids":["sec09-R21","sec09-F18","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"Frightened animal: stop and stay quiet.","fact_ids":["sec09-R21","sec09-F18","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. A driver who has just learned to warn a drifting car with the horn uses the same move on a frightened horse. The two situations need opposite responses. For a vehicle drifting toward you, you move right and warn it with your horn or lights. For a frightened animal, you stop and stay quiet rather than honking, unless stopping would cause a collision. A raised hand from a rider is the signal that the animal is frightened. So warn the car, but stop and keep quiet for the animal, and never honk or make sudden noises near it.","fact_ids":["sec09-R21","sec09-F18","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check on recovery","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Wheels off the pavement.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},{"text":"What not to do?","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you drift and your right wheels drop off the pavement onto the shoulder. What two things should you not do? The answer is do not panic and do not brake hard. Instead you slow down until you can return safely, hold the steering wheel firmly and keep the vehicle going straight, and then steer back onto the road with only as much front wheel turn as needed. A sharp turn can carry you across the road into oncoming traffic, so a gentle return is part of the same answer. Gentle is the key word for the return.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Calm responses together","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slow, straight, gentle return.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"Right and warn for a drifter.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},{"text":"Stop and stay quiet for animals.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"To finish this lesson, keep the three responses separate. If your wheels leave the road, do not panic or brake hard; slow down, hold the wheel firmly, keep going straight, and steer back with only as much turn as needed. If an oncoming vehicle drifts into your lane, move as far right as you can, slow down, warn with your horn or lights, and never swerve into the opposing lane. Near animals, watch for crossing signs, stop for a raised hand or a frightened animal unless stopping would cause a collision, and make no loud, sudden noises. If you injure a domestic animal, stop, check it and report it.","fact_ids":["sec09-F15","sec09-F16","sec09-F17","sec09-F18","sec09-F19","sec09-F20","sec09-F21","sec09-F22","sec09-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec09-u03","module_id":"sec09-m03","objective_ids":["sec09-u03"],"title":{"text":"Headlights and dimming","fact_ids":["sec09-F24","sec09-F25","sec09-F26"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Headlights are required at set times and in poor visibility, and the distances for dimming high beams are exact.","fact_ids":["sec09-F25","sec09-F26","sec09-F27","sec09-F28"]},{"text":"Parking lights and fog lights have their own rules that are easy to get wrong.","fact_ids":["sec09-F29","sec09-F30","sec09-F31"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"You are on a dark road with high beams on, following another car that is about three hundred feet ahead.","fact_ids":["sec09-F28"]},"reasoning":{"text":"You must dim your high beams when following another vehicle within three hundred fifty feet, since glare in its mirror can blind the driver.","fact_ids":["sec09-F28","sec09-R17"]},"result":{"text":"You switch to low beams because you are inside three hundred fifty feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F28"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking the dimming distance is the same for oncoming traffic and for following.","fact_ids":["sec09-R17"]},"correction":{"text":"High beams must be dimmed at five hundred feet for an oncoming vehicle but at three hundred fifty feet when you are following.","fact_ids":["sec09-R17","sec09-F27","sec09-F28"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Lights on at one thousand, dim at five hundred and three hundred fifty.","fact_ids":["sec09-R18"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A car is coming toward you while your high beams are on. At what distance must you dim them?","fact_ids":["sec09-F27"]},"answer":{"text":"Within five hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F27"]},"rationale":{"text":"When using high beams you must dim them once an oncoming vehicle is within five hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F27","sec09-R17"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Lights that keep you seen","fact_ids":["sec09-F24","sec09-F25"]},"lines":[{"text":"When headlights must be on.","fact_ids":["sec09-F24","sec09-F25"]},{"text":"When high beams must be dimmed.","fact_ids":["sec09-F24","sec09-F25"]}],"narration":{"text":"Reduced visibility, or a wet, snowy or icy road, makes driving hazardous and calls for lower speeds and longer following distances. Lights are a big part of driving safely in those conditions and at night. In this lesson we cover when your headlights must be on, the two distances at which high beams must be dimmed, what happens to fog lights when you dim, and the rules for parking lights. Every one of these rules comes with a specific time or distance, so pay attention to the numbers and to which situation each number belongs to.","fact_ids":["sec09-F24","sec09-F25"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When headlights go on","fact_ids":["sec09-F25","sec09-F26"]},"lines":[{"text":"From sunset to sunrise.","fact_ids":["sec09-F25","sec09-F26"]},{"text":"When you cannot see one thousand feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F25","sec09-F26"]}],"narration":{"text":"Headlights help others see you at any hour, and they must be on from sunset to sunrise. They must also be on whenever conditions make it hard to see people or vehicles one thousand feet ahead. So there are two tests. The first is the clock: between sunset and sunrise, headlights are required. The second is visibility: at any time of day, if conditions such as fog, smoke or heavy rain make it hard to see people or vehicles one thousand feet ahead, headlights are required as well. Either test is enough on its own to require your headlights.","fact_ids":["sec09-F25","sec09-F26"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Dimming high beams","fact_ids":["sec09-F27","sec09-F28","sec09-R17","sec09-F29"]},"lines":[{"text":"Oncoming within five hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F27","sec09-F28","sec09-R17","sec09-F29"]},{"text":"Following within three hundred fifty feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F27","sec09-F28","sec09-R17","sec09-F29"]}],"narration":{"text":"High beams must be dimmed at two different distances. When using high beams you must dim them once an oncoming vehicle is within five hundred feet. And you must dim your high beams when you are following another vehicle within three hundred fifty feet, since glare in its mirror can blind the driver. So the oncoming distance is the longer one, five hundred feet, and the following distance is the shorter one, three hundred fifty feet. Whenever you are required to dim your headlights, auxiliary lights such as fog lights must also be off.","fact_ids":["sec09-F27","sec09-F28","sec09-R17","sec09-F29"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Mixing up the distances","fact_ids":["sec09-R18","sec09-R17","sec09-F26"]},"lines":[{"text":"One thousand feet: lights on.","fact_ids":["sec09-R18","sec09-R17","sec09-F26"]},{"text":"Five hundred and three hundred fifty: dim.","fact_ids":["sec09-R18","sec09-R17","sec09-F26"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap: mixing up three different distances. The one-thousand-foot visibility test decides when headlights must be on beyond the sunset-to-sunrise rule. The five-hundred-foot and three-hundred-fifty-foot distances decide when high beams must be dimmed. Five hundred feet is for an oncoming vehicle, and three hundred fifty feet is for a vehicle you are following. So one thousand feet is about turning headlights on, not about dimming.
